title: ZLIB Compressed Data Format Specification version 3.3
summary: Defines the zlib compressed data format, a lossless format that wraps compressed data with a small header and checksum. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to squeeze a file smaller and put it back exactly the same, with a label on the box and a check that nothing broke.

questions: what is a zlib preset dictionary
how does the zlib header work
subtitle: A small wrapper that labels compressed data with a header and an Adler-32 checksum.

tldr.problem: Programs need a compressed data format that works on any CPU and operating system, handles streams of any length with bounded memory, and can be implemented without patent problems.
tldr.mechanism: A zlib stream is a 2-byte header (CMF and FLG), an optional 4-byte dictionary identifier, the compressed data (DEFLATE for method 8), and a 4-byte ADLER32 checksum of the uncompressed data.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational. It defines the wrapper and the Adler-32 checksum; a decoder that skips the checksum may suffer undetected data corruption.

facts.label: Dictionary identifier
facts.value: 4 bytes, present if FDICT is set

today: RFC 1950 is an Informational RFC and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Goals and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1950 defines a lossless compressed data format. It is meant to be independent of CPU type, operating system, file system and character set, so it can be used for interchange. Data can be produced or consumed, even for an arbitrarily long input stream, using only an a priori bounded amount of intermediate storage.

The format can use a number of different compression methods and can be implemented readily in a manner not covered by patents. It does not try to allow random access to compressed data. Its scope is in-memory compression of a sequence of arbitrary bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a packing box that works the same on every kind of computer. You can pack a huge pile of stuff a little at a time, and you get everything back exactly as it was.

sections.title: The Two-Byte Header
sections.content:
A zlib stream starts with two bytes. CMF holds the 4-bit compression method (CM) and a 4-bit compression info field (CINFO). CM = 8 means the deflate method with a window size up to 32K; CM = 15 is reserved. For CM = 8, CINFO is the base-2 logarithm of the LZ77 window size minus eight, so CINFO = 7 means a 32K window. Larger values are not allowed.

FLG holds FCHECK (bits 0 to 4), FDICT (bit 5) and FLEVEL (bits 6 to 7). FCHECK is chosen so that CMF*256 + FLG is a multiple of 31. FLEVEL for deflate says whether the compressor used the fastest (0), fast (1), default (2) or maximum compression (3) algorithm. It is not needed for decompression; it only hints whether recompression might be worthwhile.

Multi-byte numbers in this format are stored with the most-significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: The first two bytes are a luggage tag. They say how the data was packed, how big the packing table was, and include a tiny check so a damaged tag gets noticed.

sections.title: Dictionary, Data and Checksum
sections.content:
If FDICT is set, a 4-byte DICTID follows the header. A preset dictionary is a sequence of bytes fed to the compressor first without producing any output. DICTID is the Adler-32 checksum of that sequence, which lets the decompressor work out which dictionary was used. The RFC does not specify dictionary contents, because the best ones are application specific. A preset dictionary is especially useful for short inputs.

Next comes the compressed data. For method 8 it is stored in the DEFLATE format, defined in a separate document. At the end is the 4-byte ADLER32 value, computed over the uncompressed data (not including any dictionary). Any data after ADLER32 is not part of the zlib stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the packer and unpacker share a cheat sheet beforehand, which makes small things pack tighter. The tag says which cheat sheet was used, and the end of the box holds a final check number.

sections.title: The Adler-32 Checksum
sections.content:
Adler-32 is a 32-bit extension and improvement of the Fletcher checksum. It uses two sums accumulated per byte: s1 is the sum of all bytes, and s2 is the sum of all s1 values. Both are taken modulo 65521. s1 starts at 1 and s2 at 0. The checksum is s2*65536 + s1, stored most-significant byte first.

The appendix explains the design. It is much faster than CRC32 yet still gives an extremely low probability of undetected errors. 65521 is prime, which avoids a large class of two-byte errors that would leave the check unchanged. Starting s1 at 1 makes the length of the data part of s2. The RFC also gives sample C code.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker keeps two running totals as it reads every byte. The final pair of totals is like a fingerprint: change even one byte and the fingerprint will almost surely look different.

sections.title: What Compliant Software Must Do
sections.content:
A compliant compressor must produce correct CMF, FLG and ADLER32, but need not support preset dictionaries. It must not set FDICT if the surrounding format does not use preset dictionaries.

A compliant decompressor must check CMF, FLG and ADLER32 and give an error indication if any is wrong. It must also give an error if CM is not 8, and if FDICT is set and the identifier is not that of a known preset dictionary. It may ignore FLEVEL. When the other format does not use dictionaries, it must reject any stream with FDICT set.
sections.plainLanguage: The packer must write the tag and check number correctly. The unpacker must read them and shout if something is off, instead of guessing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is a single sentence: a decoder that fails to check the ADLER32 checksum value may be subject to undetected data corruption. This is why the compliance rules require decoders to verify it.
sections.plainLanguage: If you never look at the check number on the box, you might not notice the contents got broken on the way.

fields.name: CINFO
fields.desc: Base-2 log of the LZ77 window size minus eight; 7 means 32K.

fields.name: FCHECK
fields.desc: Check bits making CMF*256 + FLG a multiple of 31.
